messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan was twenty-four when he was posted to a consulate in a city that had become a battlefield. One afternoon, returning from a meeting, his armoured car lurched to a halt as a suicide bomber detonated a fuel truck fifty feet ahead. The blast wave punched through the vehicle, glass spraying, and Rohan was thrown against the door frame. He lay on the floor, ears ringing, the world a high-pitched whine, and the only thing he could smell was the sharp reek of alcohol from a shattered bottle that had rolled across his leg from the market stall the bomber had targeted. He saw the driver's face—lifeless, eyes open—and then someone pulled him out. After that image lodged in his mind, even the most ordinary things — the colour of a jacket, a car door slamming — began to feel like warnings he could no longer ignore. In the weeks that followed he could not find words to describe what he had seen; the images were too clear, too detailed, but when he tried to tell his supervisor he stammered and fell silent. Each time those images surfaced, the thought that followed was the same — that he must have done something wrong, that his carelessness had left the driver dead because of him. Because those images were so vivid and intrusive, he started noticing threads of the attack everywhere—the colour of a jacket could pull him back, or the sound of a car door closing—things that had never bothered him before suddenly became loaded with threat. The smell of alcohol, even a beer at an embassy reception, would snap him back into that moment, his nostrils filling with petrol and spirits, his heart hammering as if the bomb had just gone off. He learned to scan every room for exits, for strangers who moved too quickly, and he could not believe anyone who told him he was safe. Living in that constant state of threat, he found himself circling back to the same terrible explanation: that the attack had happened because of him, that the danger he felt was proof of his own guilt. 

What terrified Rohan most was the conviction that something about him had caused the attack—that he had been too careless, too trusting, and that the driver had died because of him. That persistent feeling of danger kept the trauma memory close to the surface, so that even in quiet moments at his desk the scene would play through his mind unbidden, as if his body needed to stay ready by replaying what had happened. He lost his faith in the people around him, in the institution he served, and in any higher power that would allow such things. The future felt hollow; he stopped making plans beyond the next hour. These appraisals made every unfamiliar face a potential threat, and each time a stranger approached him on the street or in a corridor, he felt the surge of the flashback—the heat, the ringing, the smell—and was certain this was the moment it would happen again. Once he had concluded that he was somehow responsible for the blast, every ambiguous sound or sudden movement became a potential accusation — a car door closing too hard, a colleague's laugh at the wrong moment — and he found himself scanning not just for danger but for evidence of his own guilt. He began to wear concealing clothing: long coats in warm weather, hoods pulled up, anything to shrink from notice. He took drugs at night—marijuana mostly, sometimes something stronger from a contact at a bar—to dull the memories, but the only thing that quieted the loop for a while was running until his lungs burned and his legs gave out. He pushed himself to exercise compulsively, sometimes twice a day, because exhaustion was the only state in which the flashbacks receded. Yet the reprieve never lasted; the moment his body rested, the memories surged back with greater intensity, as though the avoidance had only fed them. 

In the embassy, a colleague’s friendly tap on the shoulder could send Rohan into a frozen state, eyes unfocused, reliving the moment of impact. He knew this was irrational, and he hated himself for it, but that hatred only deepened his sense of hopelessness. His girlfriend noticed he flinched when she hugged him from behind, and he started avoiding her touch; he told her he was just tired. At work, he began arriving early and leaving late to avoid the packed elevator, and he started drinking less at functions because the alcohol smell made him leave suddenly. But feeling emotionally vulnerable—in a meeting, on the street, sitting in his own apartment—was the worst trigger, because it carried no external cue; it came from inside, and when it arrived, he would reach for a pill or go for a punishing run no matter the hour. 

The very act of hiding himself made him feel more watched, more suspicious, and the paranoia fed back into his need to conceal. Living at that pitch of alertness, he found that ordinary stimuli—a car idling too long, a door left ajar, a stranger who held his gaze a second too long—all registered as warnings, each one confirming what his body already believed. After a run, when his mind was blank, the olfactory recall would sometimes hit him without warning—the phantom smell of alcohol and diesel—and he would be back inside the memory, unable to speak. Lately, even ordinary sounds like a car backfiring or a door slamming had begun to throw him into defensive mode, his body bracing, his vision narrowing. He had come to believe that safety was a lie other people told themselves, and that he could never trust it again. 

What finally brought Rohan to therapy was a moment at a diplomatic reception when a woman accidentally knocked over a tray of glasses. The crash sent him diving under a table, shaking, in front of dozens of colleagues. He could not explain it. That night, his girlfriend found him sitting in the dark, and he told her he did not know who he was anymore. He is terrified that he is broken beyond repair, but he is also afraid that if he stops the exercise and the drugs, the memories will swallow him whole. He came because he has no other choice, and because somewhere underneath the hopelessness, he still wants to believe there is a future.
